idiom_name: immutable identity assigned once + equality, hashing and lookup by identity
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the type one immutable identity member, generated for new entities and passed in when reconstituting an entity from storage, and derive equality, hashing and lookup from that member only, never from the mutable attributes. Keep the attributes behind intention-revealing methods so the entity guards its own invariants, and let a factory or repository own identity assignment, loading and storage so the model stays persistence-ignorant. Maintain one in-memory instance per identity per unit of work (identity map) so two representations of the same entity cannot diverge; where the runtime already provides reference identity and the session guarantees a single instance, that reference identity is the realization and no equality override is needed.
code_sketch:
entity Customer
    id: CustomerId              # immutable, assigned once
    name: string                # mutable attributes; changes stay inside methods

    equals(other) = other is Customer and other.id == this.id

new_customer(name)   -> Customer(id = generate_id(), name = name)
reconstitute(row)    -> Customer(id = row.id, name = row.name)
pitfalls: Deriving equality from mutable attributes instead of identity: two representations of the same entity compare unequal after any attribute change, and a customer fetched twice becomes two customers in a set.
Assigning or mutating the identity after the entity has been used in a cache or a hash-based collection: lookups silently miss the entry and stale entries remain.
Loading the same entity twice into one session without an identity map: the two copies diverge and the last write wins by accident.
Using raw string or int as identity instead of a typed identity value object: a UserId is accidentally passed where an OrderId is expected, producing a runtime bug with no compiler warning.
Exposing public setters for entity state: callers bypass invariants that the domain methods enforce, leading to entities in invalid states (e.g., an Order with no items and status 'shipped').
Creating an entity without enforcing constructor-level invariants: a partially-initialised entity reaches a repository and is persisted in an invalid state.
Relying on ORM-generated proxies for equality: the proxy is not equal to its target entity, so hash-based collections contain the wrong entry after the entity is loaded from the database.
N+1 query performance: loading entities by following entity-to-entity associations (e.g., order.getCustomer().getAddress()) triggers a separate query per hop instead of a single batched query.

Wrong move: deriving hashCode from a database-generated id that is assigned on insert -> the hash changes when the entity transitions from transient to persistent, and it becomes unreachable in every Set and HashMap it was added to -> instead keep equals on the id (null-safe) and use a stable class-level hash (getClass().hashCode()) or an immutable business key.

Wrong move: comparing entities with getClass() != other.getClass() under Hibernate -> the lazily-loaded proxy is a generated subclass and never equals its real target, so entities fetched through associations silently vanish from sets -> instead compare with an instanceof check (or Hibernate.getClass()) and delegate to the identifier.

Wrong move: handing every domain concept an id because its relational table has a primary key -> the model becomes a web of mutable, lifecycle-tracked objects where identity adds id-generation, locking and tracking cost without guarding any invariant -> instead model attribute clusters as value objects and reserve entity status for concepts whose continuity or invariants genuinely require identity.
sources: Erard, Stéphane. Part 31: Entity — Identity Continuity Over Time (2025) — https://serard.dev/content/blog/ts-ddd/31-entity.html
Enterprise Craftsmanship — Entity Identity vs Database Primary Key — https://enterprisecraftsmanship.com/posts/entity-identity-vs-database-primary-key/
